title: Steam blocking
subtitle: Setting stitch definition and dimensions with a steam iron.
excerpt: Steam blocking uses a steam iron held above the finished piece to relax the fibres and fix the shape without submerging the work in water. It works particularly well on wool-blend yarns, cables, and textured stitches where wet blocking might flatten the surface.
sourceNotes: Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), finishing chapter. General UK textile finishing practice documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter finishing notes.
heroPrompt: Close-up of a steam iron held a few centimetres above a pinned knitted swatch on a blocking mat, steam rising gently.

glossaryTerms.definition: A finishing technique in which steam from an iron is held above a pinned knitted piece to relax fibres and set the shape without wetting the fabric.

content.text: uses the heat and moisture from a steam iron to relax knitted fibres and set the dimensions of a finished piece. Unlike wet blocking, it does not require submerging the work, which makes it faster and better suited to textured stitches such as cables and seed stitch, where full saturation might flatten the relief. It works well on wool, wool-blend, and many plant-fibre yarns. Difficulty: beginner.
A steam iron with a good steam output
A foam blocking mat or padded ironing board
A damp pressing cloth for fibres that dislike direct steam

attrs.title: Never touch the iron to the knitting
attrs.body: The iron must hover above the surface at all times. Direct contact flattens the stitches permanently and can scorch the yarn. Acrylic yarns cannot be steam blocked; heat melts the fibres. Check the yarn label for heat tolerance before proceeding.

content.text: Pin the piece to the blocking mat, easing it to the finished dimensions stated in the pattern. Use plenty of pins along the edges.
Fill the iron with water and set it to the steam setting appropriate for the fibre. Wool sits at a medium heat; cotton can tolerate a higher setting.
Hold the iron approximately 2-3 cm above the surface and press the steam button. Move the iron slowly across the piece in overlapping passes without ever letting it touch the fabric.
After steaming, gently pat the piece back into shape if any pinned edges have shifted. Re-pin where needed.
Leave the piece pinned in place until fully cool and dry, which takes 30-60 minutes depending on the yarn weight.

Steam blocking is the preferred finishing method for cabled panels, ribbed neckbands, and textured accessories where wet blocking risks crushing the stitch relief. It is also useful for joining pieces before seaming, as a gentle pass of steam helps two edges align cleanly.

items.symptom: Cables and texture have been flattened
items.cause: The iron touched the surface, or the steam was held too close
items.fix: Keep the iron at least 2 cm above the fabric. For heavily textured stitches, use a damp pressing cloth as a buffer between the iron and the knitting.

items.symptom: Piece has not relaxed or changed shape at all
items.cause: Insufficient steam, or an acrylic yarn that does not respond to steam
items.fix: Increase the steam output and pass the iron more slowly. If the yarn is acrylic, switch to a damp-cloth method or accept that steam blocking will not set the shape.

items.symptom: Yarn feels stiff or crunchy after blocking
items.cause: Too much heat or the iron was held in one spot for too long
items.fix: Keep the iron moving constantly. Allow the piece to cool completely before unpin; stiffness usually softens as the yarn cools fully.

items.cause: Not enough pins, or they were placed too far apart
items.fix: Use more pins at closer intervals, particularly on curved or diagonal edges. Pin every 2-3 cm for precise shaping.
